text:
The trade off IS performance, if you run a UV at low voltages.
For a hypothetical gpu silicon to hit lets say 2000 Mhz it requires 1000mV, and the temperature limit for this is 70C, - If a stock gpu was targeting that 2000Mhz with a 1150mV voltage, it would run at ~74C, which would be higher than the temperature target and not allow to hit the clock target hanging around lets say ~1900Mhz.

In this hypothetical you would UV your card from the stock 1150mV to the best possible voltages, which would be 1000mV and allow you to run at the maximum boost clock of 2000Mhz. This is what you would do on Pascal/Polaris/Vega cards because they didn't hold boosts very well unless you had higher fan speeds or raised the power/temp limits.
The other "trade off" is that you don't get to OC at the silicons max capacity.

Ampere might differ, so does any other architecture, so only tinkering gives the correct answer!

author: @RobBCactive

text: @RobBCactive  bits themselves are analog. There is a threshold for response where a bit is on or off. Error checking is built in to caches and buses to ensure loss is minimal, but they work within a threshold of tolerance. That tolerance is set at a given charge who’s energy is provided constantly from a source but modulated (divided) but internal clocks. Lower power too much and it fails to function entirely. In between, you have a band where it can function, but there are errors. Above that is stability. Above that for any given card is the rated stability, which is the MHz that the card is offered at. There is some wiggle room, but not so much, especially in the age of binning and aftermarket fine tuning. But the “tolerable” level of error is high when the output is visual, and the errors might only express themselves in subtle shifts of color in some small number of pixels each frame.

text:
Because their cards need to run perfect all the time for years to come. Furthermore silicon quality differences also matter, one gpu might be able to run 20mV lower than another. And as the gpu ages it might need slightly more voltage to be stable and they don't want their gpu's all starting to crash after a couple of years. Instead they just give it some extra voltage and that ensures it will never crash no matter what. 

They don't have the time to stability test every gpu, just shipping it with the voltage required for the worst gpu die is cheaper, but yes that does mean that you can nearly always lower the stock voltage a bit to save some power, CO2 emissions and noise.

Edit: AMD did actually bother with this for their Radeon VII, they had wildly different stock voltages. You can find some examples in this community spread sheet: https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1Iim9e_ejX3nkgxLIZ3vLu1seQ1m0lDTKUhClJpAO-Gk/edit#gid=0
